title: Low & Predictable Latency
summary: Getting alarms, voice and video through on time, every time, not just on average.

opener.promise: Alarms and calls on time, not just on average
opener.problem: Now and then an alarm waits behind a large download before reaching the nurses’ station.

beats.heading: The alarm stuck behind a download

caption.headline: The alarm stuck behind a download
caption.takeaway: Most alarms arrive at once; a few wait behind downloads, and those late ones matter most.
caption.technical: 802.11be’s scope includes improved worst-case [[latency|latency]] and [[jitter|jitter]]{{be-latency-objective}}; [[tail-latency|tail latency]] is the slowest messages’ delay.

beats.body:
A bedside monitor raises an alarm. Its message is tiny, but it shares the channel with a workstation pulling a large image. Most of the time it gets through almost instantly; now and then it waits much longer.

Those rare late messages, the [[tail-latency|tail]], are what matter for alarms, voice and remote procedures. Wi-Fi 7 was designed to cut them: the scope of IEEE 802.11be includes improved worst-case [[latency|latency]] and [[jitter|jitter]] {{be-latency-objective}}.
beats.bottomLine: For alarms, voice and remote procedures, the rare slow message matters more than the typical one.
beats.sceneDescription: A road runs from a bedside monitor to the nurses’ station. Each alarm is an ambulance; a large download is a line of grey trucks on the same single lane. Most ambulances drive straight through, but now and then one gets stuck behind a truck. Each arrival adds a block to an arrivals board behind the road: a tall green column on the left for alarms on time, and a trail of red blocks to the right for the few that arrived late, labelled the tail. The board is labelled illustrative.

callout.title: Why some alarms arrive late
points: Alarms share the channel with large downloads
Most arrive at once; a few wait behind a download
Those late alarms are the ones that matter{{be-latency-objective}}

questions.q: How much lower is Wi-Fi 7 latency?
questions.a: There is no single figure: worst-case delay depends on load, device mix and configuration. The standard targets improved worst-case latency and jitter{{be-latency-objective}}; measure it in a pilot with your own alarm and voice systems.

beats.heading: Wi-Fi 7 clears the way

caption.headline: Wi-Fi 7 clears the way
caption.takeaway: A second band and protected [[twt|TWT]] slots keep downloads out of the alarm’s path{{rtwt-protect}}.
caption.technical: [[mlo|MLO]] uses whichever link wins access first{{mlo-tid-mapping}}; restricted service periods clear the air{{rtwt-protect}}.

beats.body: Wi-Fi 7 removes the reasons an alarm waits. **[[mlo|Multi-link operation]]** sends it on whichever band is free {{mlo-bands}}. **[[restricted-twt|Restricted TWT]]**, a form of [[twt|Target Wake Time]], reserves protected time, and other devices pause before it starts {{rtwt-protect}}. **[[multi-ru|Multi-RU]]** fits urgent traffic into spare parts of the channel {{multi-ru-be}}.
beats.bottomLine: Each feature removes a different reason urgent messages wait.
beats.deepDive: MLO lets traffic move to the link that gains channel access first, with TID-to-link mapping steering traffic classes {{mlo-tid-mapping}}. Restricted TWT service periods require supporting stations to end transmissions before the period starts {{rtwt-protect}}. Multi-RU allows flexible RU combinations per station {{multi-ru-be}}. Each one addresses a different cause of queuing delay.
beats.sceneDescription: Wi-Fi 7’s road has two lanes, standing for two bands. An ambulance takes whichever lane has no download ahead. At regular protected slots the trucks pull over onto the shoulder and stop, so any ambulance passes straight through. The new arrivals board fills with green blocks on the left and almost no red.

questions.a: It depends on the cause. MLO helps when one band is congested{{mlo-tid-mapping}}, Restricted TWT when long transmissions block urgent traffic{{rtwt-protect}}, and Multi-RU when the channel has spare fragments{{multi-ru-be}}.

callout.title: How Wi-Fi 7 clears the way
points: [[restricted-twt|Restricted TWT]]: downloads pause in protected slots{{rtwt-protect}}
[[multi-ru|Multi-RU]]: urgent traffic fits into spare room{{multi-ru-be}}

beats.heading: A shorter tail, alarms on time

caption.headline: A shorter tail, alarms on time
caption.takeaway: Wi-Fi 7 cuts the late tail{{latency-histogram-illustrative}}; test worst-case delay before rollout.
caption.technical: Results vary with load, device mix and configuration; pilot latency-sensitive applications before rollout{{be-latency-objective}}.

beats.body:
Side by side, with the same alarms and downloads: the earlier generation leaves a trail of late alarms; Wi-Fi 7 keeps them bunched on time. The boards show the shape of the change, not measured values {{latency-histogram-illustrative}}.

Wireless is one link in the alarm chain, so include worst-case delay in acceptance tests and keep alarm systems in their manufacturers’ validated configurations.
beats.bottomLine: Include worst-case latency in Wi-Fi 7 acceptance testing for alarm, voice and video, not only average throughput.
beats.deepDive: Worst-case latency depends on deployment: channel load, device mix, client support for MLO and restricted TWT, and configuration of traffic classes. No figures are shown here because results vary by environment; evaluate latency-sensitive applications in a pilot before rollout {{latency-histogram-illustrative}}.
beats.sceneDescription: Two roads, one above the other, with the same alarms and downloads. Above, the earlier generation: one lane, and its arrivals board has a trail of red late arrivals. Below, Wi-Fi 7: two lanes and protected slots, and its board is bunched on the left with almost no tail, labelled alarms arrive on time, consistently. Both boards are labelled illustrative.

callout.title: What to test
points: Worst-case delay for alarms, voice and video, not averages
Busy-hour tests with real downloads running
Alarm systems in their manufacturers’ validated configurations

questions.q: Can we rely on Wi-Fi 7 for clinical alarms?
questions.a: Wi-Fi is one link in the alarm chain. Wi-Fi 7 improves consistency, but alarm systems should still follow their manufacturers’ validated configurations and your clinical engineering testing.
